title: Pauri 34, sound: raatee rutee
tomorrow: Pauri 34, meaning: a place for dharma

lines: A CALENDAR ON THE KITCHEN WALL.
cards: A calendar hangs on the kitchen wall in many Punjabi homes. It isn't just days and months. In small type are the moon's phases, the full-moon days, the first day of each month when many families go to the gurdwara.

Grandparents read it like the weather: this is a good day for that, the full moon is Thursday. Time, on that wall, has layers. The night, the season, the moon, the day of the week, all stacked on top of each other.
Pauri 34 opens with that stack, four words long, and it sounds like a clock ticking.

teach.b: Raatee rutee thitee vaar. Four words, four kinds of time. Raatee: nights.
Rutee: seasons; a rut is a season, the way the monsoon or the cold season comes around.
Thitee: lunar days. A thit is one day of the moon's month, counted from new moon to full, the small print on that kitchen calendar.
Vaar: the days of the week, still heard in weekday names across North India: Somvaar, Mangalvaar, and so on. In four words, Nanak lays down the whole clock: night, season, moon, week. Now the sound.
Raatee, rutee, thitee: the same shape, a short first beat and a long ee, like three ticks. Then vaar, open and long, like the chime.

teach.h: PAVAN PAANEE AGANEE — AIR, WATER, FIRE.
teach.b: Then the line turns from time to things: pavan paanee aganee paataal. Air, water, fire, and the regions below. Pavan, paanee: two p's, soft as breath.
Aganee: fire, a cousin of the Sanskrit agni. Paataal: the underworlds, the depths. First the clock, then the elements.
Tomorrow, what Nanak sets in the middle of all this, and the job he gives it.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 34 begins the stanzas many teachers describe as the realms, opening with a line that names night, season, lunar day and weekday.

o: a holy festival day of the year
the days of the moon's month, lunar days
the days of the week, Monday to Sunday

games.q: the sound of Pauri 34 — tap the pairs.

s: the first four words of Pauri 34 are four kinds of time
night, season, lunar day and weekday.
vaar still names weekdays in North India
the second half of the line keeps listing kinds of time
it turns to the elements: air, water, fire and the depths.

games.q: Pauri 34 lays down night, season, moon and week, then air, water and fire. what's it setting up?
o: a place in the middle of it all, with a job.
a warning about the end of time.
games.why: in the middle of time and the elements, Nanak sets something down and gives it a purpose. that's tomorrow.

practice: Say the first line aloud three times, raatee rutee thitee vaar, pavan paanee aganee paataal: tick on the first three words, chime on vaar, then let the second half flow like breath.
Afterward, sit and notice what time it is for you, in layers: day or night, which season outside, which day of the week. Let the answers come and settle, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Thitee, the lunar days. It opens with the whole clock in four words, nights, seasons, moon-days and weekdays, and then the elements: air, water, fire and the depths.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 34: nights, seasons, lunar days, weekdays.

carryVoice: Your line: raatee rutee, nights and seasons. The whole clock fits in four words. Two hundred twenty days now.
